sentences.text: The animal possessed a robust humerus measuring 1.69 meters in length with a large deltopectoral crest.
Its tail vertebrae were wider than tall and lacked pleurocoels.
The sacral vertebrae also lacked pleurocoels, which are large air-filled spaces found in other titanosaurs.
One proximal caudal vertebra features a convex rear articular condyle.
The scapula possesses a medial concavity bordered by a prominent rugosity, a feature shared with other titanosaurs.
Paralititan was described by American paleontologist Joshua B. Smith and colleagues in 2001.
Fossils were found by an American expedition in the Bahariya Oasis, western Egypt.
An incomplete dorsal vertebra described by Ernst Stromer in 1932 was later assigned to the species.
Researcher Joshua Smith rediscovered the fossil site Gebel el Dist in 1999, where Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf had worked between 1912 and 1914.
Recent estimates suggest the animal was about 26 meters long and weighed between 30 and 55 tonnes.
Only 5.1% of the skeleton is known, making exact size estimates difficult.
American paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter estimated the length at around 26 meters in a 2006 study.
It coexisted with dinosaurs including the sauropod Aegyptosaurus and theropods such as Tameryraptor, Spinosaurus, and Bahariasaurus.
Paralititan is classified as a member of the family Saltasauridae within the superfamily Titanosauria.
It belongs to the Lithostrotia group, which existed during the Cretaceous period on all continents except Australia.
The species is classified as a member of the subfamily Saltasaurinae, specifically within an Afro-European clade alongside Abditosaurus.
Smith and colleagues originally classified it within the now-unused clade Titanosauridae.
The animal lived in present-day Egypt during the Late Cretaceous period.
The Bahariya Formation where fossils were found dates to the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
During the Cenomanian, the formation was located on the margin of the Tethys Sea and consisted of mangrove swamps, rivers, and tidal flats.
Paralititan is the first dinosaur confirmed to have inhabited a mangrove habitat.
It is debated whether several isolated sauropod fossils previously assigned to Aegyptosaurus actually belong to Paralititan.
Researchers suggest that the presence of a large Carcharodontosaurus tooth near the skeleton indicates the sauropod was scavenged by the carnivore.
Because little is known about the animal, its exact size is difficult to estimate.
